transcript:
# Day 3, Game Theory and Decisions: What a game is - players, strategies, payoffs, and why this matters outside games (von Neumann and Morgenstern, 1944)

Two banks are bidding for the same corporate client. Each has to decide, this week, whether to cut its fee. If one cuts and the other does not, the cutter wins the account. If both cut, they split a smaller pie. If neither cuts, they keep healthy margins and the client picks on relationship. Notice what makes this hard: your best move depends on what the other bank does, and their best move depends on what they think you will do. That loop is the whole subject of game theory.

A game, in this sense, is any situation where the outcome for each person depends on the choices of more than one person. It has three parts. Players are the people or organizations making choices: the two banks. Strategies are the complete plans of action available to each player: cut or hold. Payoffs are what each player gets for each combination of choices, usually written as numbers in a table so you can see all four outcomes at once. That is it. No dice, no board. A game is just interdependent decision making, written down carefully enough that you can reason about it.

The reason to write it down is that your intuition tends to see only your own column. You ask "what should I do?" when the better question is "what will they do, given what they expect me to do?" The table forces you to put yourself in the other chair. A salary negotiation, a merger, a sibling deciding who calls Mom, a squadron choosing whether to request more fuel before the other squadron does: all of these are games, and most of them are being played badly because nobody wrote down the other side's payoffs.

The field was formalized in 1944 when John von Neumann, a mathematician, and Oskar Morgenstern, an economist, published Theory of Games and Economic Behavior. Von Neumann had earlier proved a result for strictly competitive two player games, but the book argued that the same machinery could describe markets, bargaining and politics. Within a few years it was being used at the RAND Corporation to think about nuclear strategy, which is where it earned both its fame and its reputation for coldness.

The strongest objection is that real people do not behave like the players in the models. Classic game theory assumes each player knows the payoffs, reasons perfectly, and cares only about their own result. Experiments since the 1970s show people cooperate when the model says they should defect, punish unfairness at a cost to themselves, and misjudge what others want. Critics say the theory describes a species that does not exist. Defenders give two answers. First, the models are not predictions but tools for seeing structure: even if you will not play the "rational" move, knowing what it is tells you what you are giving up. Second, the field adapted, and behavioral game theory now builds fairness, limited reasoning and habit into the payoffs. That is a fair reply, though it concedes that the elegant early version oversold itself.

This is the first reading in this track, so the link runs sideways. On Day 2 you met Sun Tzu insisting that a commander calculate before battle. He was doing game theory without the vocabulary: weighing his own position against the enemy's, and asking how each would respond to the other. Later in this track we will see Thomas Schelling make that connection explicit.

A question for today: pick one decision you face at work this week and write down, even roughly, who the other players are and what they get from each outcome. Does the table change what you would do?

Optional source: von Neumann and Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, chapter 1, sections 1 and 2, where they lay out why economics needs a theory of games at all.
